title: Overview and prerequisites
content:
AUREL is a demo restaurant website with a dark and gold look. Visitors browse a 100-dish menu, view venue photos with credited sources, and send a table request or a message. Staff sign in with Cognito accounts in the admin group to manage the data. This workshop is a team project of our FCAJ group.
Technology
Frontend: Next.js 15.5.28, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zod, Node.js 22, pnpm 11.25.0. Backend in Singapore (ap-southeast-1): API Gateway HTTP API, Lambda (arm64, 256 MB, 20 s timeout), DynamoDB on-demand, Cognito, S3 and SES. Amplify Hosting serves the Next.js app with server-side rendering. Business rule: a new reservation is only a request with status pending. Staff confirm or cancel it later, so a successful form submission does not mean the table is confirmed.
Completion criteria (expected outputs)
A 7-page website whose forms work against the backend. A 100-dish menu with self-hosted WebP images. Public and admin APIs with clear access boundaries. A transaction that protects seat capacity per time slot and a UUID that prevents duplicate requests. Infrastructure templates, deployment steps, tests, monitoring and clean-up guidance. Known limits: SES is still in the sandbox, there is no outbox or queue for emails, the admin MFA screen is not built, capacity is counted per start time only, and the venue photos are reference material rather than photos of a real AUREL restaurant.
Source code: https://github.com/ndthuy21/aurel-restaurant · Live site: https://main.d2rkhtb7c0k5r7.amplifyapp.com/
Prerequisites Accounts and access
A dedicated AWS lab account in ap-southeast-1. Do not reuse stack names from another project. Permissions for CloudFormation, IAM, DynamoDB, S3, Cognito, SES, Lambda, API Gateway, Amplify, CodeCommit and CloudWatch. An email address that you own, used as SenderEmail and verified in SES. Tools
Node.js 22.13 or later and pnpm 11.25.0 (Corepack). AWS CLI v2 and Python 3 (helper scripts for the admin user and monitoring). Git. On Windows, run the shell commands in WSL or Git Bash, or convert the variable syntax to PowerShell. Rules: never put AWS keys or passwords in the source code, and use your own resource IDs instead of the demo ones.

title: IAM for beginners: if an access key leaks, what is the maximum damage?
content:
Original post (AWS Study Group): https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2333529884078637/
When I first started learning AWS, I usually did everything with a single account that had full permissions. That is convenient until I asked myself: if an access key on my machine or on GitHub leaks, what can whoever finds it do? That question led me to AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
The first point is telling the types of identities apart. The root user has the highest level of access in the account, and AWS recommends using it only for a few tasks that require it, with MFA enabled. Day-to-day work should use another identity that is granted just enough permissions.
The second point is the type of credentials. Long-term access keys are convenient but risky, because they never expire on their own and can linger in source code, configuration files, or commit history. For people, AWS recommends signing in through IAM Identity Center. For applications running on AWS (EC2, Lambda), use an IAM role to get temporary credentials. The trade-off is that the initial setup is slightly more complex, but in return there is no fixed key to leak.
The third point is the principle of least privilege. Instead of attaching a policy that allows every action on every resource, we allow only the exact actions on the exact resources that are needed. The figure below illustrates this: an IAM user and an IAM role share one policy that allows s3:GetObject but denies s3:DeleteObject on an S3 bucket. According to AWS policy evaluation logic, an explicit deny always wins over an allow, so it can be used to block sensitive actions.
I will verify this with a small lab rather than rely on conclusions from theory:
Create two IAM identities, one with broad permissions and one with narrow permissions. Run the same set of AWS CLI commands with both: list buckets, read an object, delete an object, create an EC2 instance. Record which commands succeed and which are denied (AccessDenied). Use IAM Access Analyzer to see which permissions or access keys were granted but never used. Note: analyzing unused access requires creating a separate unused access analyzer, and it is charged by the number of IAM users and roles analyzed each month, so I check the pricing page first and delete the analyzer when I finish. The result of step 3 shows the real “blast radius” if each identity’s key were leaked.
For operations, I will enable MFA, rotate or delete unused access keys, keep keys out of source code, and regularly review overly broad policies. When the lab ends, temporary users, roles, and keys must be deleted.
My takeaway: least privilege does not prevent a key from leaking, but it limits the consequences when an incident happens. The actual limit depends on the specific policy, so it needs to be tested as above before drawing a conclusion.
References:
Security best practices in IAM: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html IAM roles: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html Policy evaluation logic (explicit deny): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html IAM Access Analyzer: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html #AWS #AWSStudyGroup #FCAJ #FirstCloudAIJourney #IAM #CloudSecurity #LeastPrivilege

title: Architecture and data flow
content:
Visitor flow
The browser loads pages, scripts, images and fonts from Amplify Hosting over HTTPS. GET /menu goes straight to API Gateway; Lambda queries the menu partition and returns the dishes that are available. POST /reservations is validated for schema, consent, a honeypot field, IP and email limits, and the Vietnam date and time. DynamoDB saves the request and increases the seat counter in one transaction (maximum 24 seats per slot). Sending the same UUID again returns the stored request without adding seats. After a new request is saved, Lambda tries to send an acknowledgement email through SES. If the email fails, the request is still stored. SES is in the sandbox, so only verified addresses or the mailbox simulator receive mail. POST /contact stores the message. Visitor data cannot be read through the public API. Admin and media flow
The browser sends the sign-in to the Next.js BFF, which authenticates with Cognito and keeps the access token in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie (Secure when deployed). The BFF forwards it in the Authorization header. The API Gateway JWT authorizer checks signature, issuer, audience and expiry; Lambda also checks token_use=access and the admin group. Dish photos (JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 2 MB) go through the BFF and API Gateway to Lambda, which stores them under menu-images/ in a private S3 bucket and saves the path in DynamoDB. When a visitor views the menu, Lambda returns a signed GET URL for the current image version. Arrow 7 in the diagram: Lambda writes dish images to the private S3 media bucket with its IAM execution role, and the browser reads them with a signed GET URL. A separate test page /admin/media uses signed PUT (120 s) and GET (900 s) URLs, and files under uploads/ expire after 30 days. DynamoDB model: one on-demand table with encryption and point-in-time recovery.
pk sk Content menu dish ID Menu items, public query reservations UUID Reservation data and status, admin only contacts UUID Messages, admin only slots date#time Seat counter with conditional update limits hash + time bucket Request counters with TTL Deployment flow: a Git push to the main branch of the private CodeCommit repository triggers an Amplify build that publishes the frontend and the BFF. The backend is deployed separately with CloudFormation; a separate S3 bucket holds the Lambda package. CloudWatch collects logs and metrics.

title: Proposal
content:
1. Overview of the problem and solution Small restaurants often show their dishes on social media but take bookings through scattered channels. Staff struggle to collect requests, guests do not know whether a request arrived, and menu changes are made by hand in several places. AUREL brings these flows into one web application with centralized data, built on AWS serverless services (Next.js, API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, Cognito, S3 and SES). It is a team project with source code and a working deployment: https://main.d2rkhtb7c0k5r7.amplifyapp.com/
2. Objectives and scope Objectives: show the restaurant and its menu, receive table requests with a clear status, let staff manage the menu and requests, and give operators logs, metrics and alarms.
In scope: home, menu, venue photos, about, contact, reservation and admin pages; menu CRUD; reservation status updates; dish photo upload to S3; acknowledgement email within the SES sandbox.
Out of scope: payments, POS, physical table maps, overlapping dining durations, customer accounts, multiple branches and commercial SLA.
3. Problem to solve Reservations are spread over several channels, guests get no clear acknowledgement, and staff edit the menu manually. The solution gives one place to receive requests, protect seat capacity, update the menu and observe the system.
4. Preliminary solution architecture Visitors load the site from Amplify Hosting and call API Gateway for the menu, reservations and contact. Admin sign-in goes through the Next.js BFF to Cognito, and admin requests pass a JWT authorizer. Lambda stores data in DynamoDB, sends acknowledgement emails through SES and keeps dish photos in a private S3 bucket. CloudWatch collects logs and metrics. See section 5.3 for details.
5. Plan and timeline Phase Output Milestone Design and local development Pages, service layer, input validation, tests Code and test results, 02–03/11 AWS deployment Three application stacks, Cognito admin, seeded data Evidence on 03/11 Content completion Vietnamese fonts, 100 dishes, venue photos Amplify jobs 3–5 succeeded Documentation and operations Bilingual report, diagram, monitoring, cost estimate CloudWatch and Pricing Calculator evidence Personal review and submission Own diagram, event photos, blog links In progress 6. Cost estimation Assumptions: 10,000 visits, 100,000 API requests and 100,000 SSR requests per month, 20 GB of delivered content, Lambda 256 MB at 200 ms, 1,000 emails and 5 admin users, Singapore Region, USD, before tax and free tier.
Item Monthly cost (USD) AWS Pricing Calculator workload estimate (20 usage lines, 8 services) about 6.00 Independent budget model, including allowances for transfer, dashboard and CodeCommit 12.17 Independent budget with a 25% reserve 15.21 The two figures differ because the independent model adds allowances (dashboard, data transfer, CodeCommit, report build) and uses conservative rates. Neither is a bill, and the Calculator figure covers only the 20 entered lines. Not yet included: WAF, NAT, SQS, custom domain, paid support and restore or export of DynamoDB.
7. Risks and mitigation Risk Impact Mitigation SES sandbox Unverified guests get no email Save the request first, state the limit, request production access when appropriate Email fails after the database write Request exists without an email Staff still see it; an outbox with SQS and a DLQ is proposed Seat contention Over-booking Transaction with conditional counter update API abuse Higher load and cost Validation, honeypot, limiter and throttling; no WAF yet Broad account permissions Larger blast radius Resource-scoped runtime roles; operate outside the root user Retained resources Charges continue after stack deletion Inventory, backup and controlled manual clean-up

title: Learning AWS without burning your wallet: easy-to-forget charges when doing labs
content:
Original post (AWS Study Group): https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2333732477391711/
When I started doing labs, what worried me most was not a wrong configuration but the bill at the end of the month. My question was: which services can cost money unexpectedly, and how do I spot it early?
The charges that are easy to forget usually come from resources that are “idle but still billed”. An EC2 instance left running is the most obvious example. A NAT Gateway is billed for every hour it exists and for every GB of data that passes through it, partial hours are rounded up to a full hour, and to stop being charged you must delete the NAT Gateway entirely. An EBS volume is still charged for storage while its instance is stopped, and a volume detached from an instance is still charged until it is deleted. A public IPv4 address can also incur hourly charges, even when it is not in use. Exact prices vary by Region and over time, so I always check the official AWS pricing page before drawing conclusions.
To see where the money goes, I use AWS Cost Explorer and group costs by tag. To do that, tags must be applied when the resources are created, for example project=lab, and then activated as cost allocation tags in Billing and Cost Management. According to the AWS documentation, a tag can take up to 24 hours to appear and up to another 24 hours to activate. Cost data for the current period can also be updated with a delay of more than 24 hours, so Cost Explorer is not a real-time alerting tool.
To be warned in advance, I use AWS Budgets. I set a small monthly budget and configure email alerts for when actual or forecasted cost reaches a certain threshold. The trade-off is that, as AWS notes, costs or usage can exceed the threshold before Budgets manages to notify, and Budgets only alerts and does not stop resources by itself.
I will verify this with a small experiment:
Build a lab with a few resources and apply consistent tags. Record the daily cost in Cost Explorer. Compare two scenarios: cleaning up right after the lab versus leaving everything running for a few days. Note the difference and the time from when a charge occurs to when the alert arrives. For operations, I keep a cleanup checklist after every session: stop or delete EC2, delete NAT Gateways, delete unused volumes and snapshots, release Elastic IPs. I also check other Regions, because resources created by mistake in an unfamiliar Region are very easy to forget.
My takeaway: monitoring tools help detect problems early, but the habit of cleaning up is what keeps the bill low. The actual savings can only be concluded once there is data from my own account.
References:
Analyzing your costs and usage with AWS Cost Explorer: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-what-is.html Exploring your data using Cost Explorer (data latency): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-exploring-data.html Managing your costs with AWS Budgets: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/budgets-managing-costs.html Activating user-defined cost allocation tags: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/activating-tags.html Amazon VPC pricing (NAT Gateway, public IPv4): https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/ Why am I charged for Amazon EBS when all my instances are stopped?: https://www.repost.aws/knowledge-center/ebs-charge-stopped-instance #AWS #AWSStudyGroup #FCAJ #FirstCloudAIJourney #CostOptimization #AWSBudgets #CostExplorer

title: Step-by-step lab guide
content:
Step 1 — Run and check locally Run the application on your own machine first, so that the code, the tests and the data model are known to work before anything is created on AWS.
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm setup pnpm dev pnpm check && pnpm build && pnpm test:smoke pnpm setup creates a local .env.local; do not commit it.
Expected result: pnpm check and pnpm build finish without errors, the smoke suite passes, and the site opens locally with the menu loaded.
Step 2 — Deploy the AWS backend The backend is deployed with CloudFormation in two stacks: aurel-artifacts for the package bucket and aurel-backend for the API, database, authentication and media storage.
export AWS_PROFILE=aurel-lab AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1 export SENDER_EMAIL='YOUR_OWN_VERIFIED_EMAIL' pnpm build:lambda aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name aurel-artifacts --template-file infra/artifacts.yaml export ARTIFACT_BUCKET=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name aurel-artifacts \ --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey==`BucketName`].OutputValue | [0]' --output text) aws cloudformation package --template-file infra/template.yaml \ --s3-bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" --s3-prefix lambda --output-template-file packaged-backend.yaml aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name aurel-backend --template-file packaged-backend.yaml \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND \ --parameter-overrides FrontendOrigin=https://pending.invalid SenderEmail="$SENDER_EMAIL" aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name aurel-backend --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs' --output table Confirm the verification email from AWS while the stack is being created. Then seed the menu and create the admin user:
export TABLE_NAME=YOUR_TABLE_OUTPUT node dist/seed-aws.mjs python3 bootstrap-admin.py --pool YOUR_USER_POOL_ID --email YOUR_ADMIN_EMAIL The seed script only adds missing dishes and can be run again. The admin script asks for the password interactively, adds the user to the admin group and does not allow self-registration. Quick check:
curl -i "$API_URL/menu" # 200 curl -i "$API_URL/admin/reservations" # 401 Expected result: the aurel-backend stack reaches CREATE_COMPLETE and prints its outputs (ApiUrl, table, buckets, user pool). /menu returns 200 with the 100 seeded dishes, and /admin/reservations returns 401 without a token.
Step 3 — Frontend and CI/CD python3 scripts/package-source.py --output ../aurel-codecommit-source.zip aws s3 cp ../aurel-codecommit-source.zip "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/source/aurel-lab.zip" aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name aurel-frontend --template-file infra/amplify-codecommit.yaml \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM --parameter-overrides SourceBucket="$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \ SourceKey=source/aurel-lab.zip ApiUrl="$API_URL" CognitoClientId="$COGNITO_CLIENT_ID" \ CognitoUserPoolId="$USER_POOL_ID" The template creates a CodeCommit repository, a read-only role and the Amplify app. Use these environment variables (never admin passwords, session secrets or AWS keys):
Variable Value DATA_MODE aws API_BASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL ApiUrl, no trailing slash COGNITO_CLIENT_ID, COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID backend outputs APP_AWS_REGION ap-southeast-1 APP_ORIGIN exact frontend origin Then set the real frontend origin in the backend and start an Amplify job:
aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name aurel-backend --template-file packaged-backend.yaml \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND \ --parameter-overrides FrontendOrigin="$FRONTEND_ORIGIN" SenderEmail="$SENDER_EMAIL" aws amplify start-job --app-id "$APP_ID" --branch-name main --job-type RELEASE aws amplify list-jobs --app-id "$APP_ID" --branch-name main --max-results 5 Treat the deployment as successful only when the job status is SUCCEED. The ZIP seeds the repository only once; later updates are Git pushes to main, which Amplify builds automatically.
Expected result: the Amplify job ends with status SUCCEED, the website opens at its Amplify address, the menu loads from the API without CORS errors, and an admin can sign in.

title: CloudTrail and GuardDuty: how do you know who did what in an AWS account?
content:
Original post (AWS Study Group): https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2334665957298363/
After learning about IAM, I had a follow-up question: if someone uses my key, how do I know what they did and when? That question led me to AWS CloudTrail and Amazon GuardDuty.
CloudTrail records API calls in the account, whether they come from the console, the CLI, or an SDK. Each event shows who made the call, what was called, from which IP address, at what time, and whether it succeeded. By default, the Event history page lets you view management events from the last 90 days in each Region, and viewing is free of charge. To keep a continuous record beyond 90 days, you need to create a trail that delivers logs to S3. AWS recommends using a multi-Region trail so that no activity is missed. The trade-off is that one copy of management events delivered to S3 is not charged by CloudTrail, but I still pay for S3 storage and am responsible for protecting the bucket that holds the logs.
GuardDuty does a different job. It is a threat detection service that continuously analyzes data sources such as CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs, and then produces findings with a severity from 1.0 to 8.9, where High falls between 7.0 and 8.9. The difference is that CloudTrail gives you raw data to investigate on your own, while GuardDuty proactively alerts you to anything unusual. The two services complement rather than replace each other. The first time GuardDuty is enabled in a Region, the account gets a 30-day trial in that Region; after the trial, usage-based charges apply, so I check the pricing page and set a calendar reminder before the trial ends.
I will verify this with an incident-simulation lab, making use of my digital forensics knowledge:
Create a lab IAM user and use that user’s key to run a few CLI commands, including one that is deliberately denied. Find these events in CloudTrail Event history by user name or event name. Record the time, source IP, and the AccessDenied error code to build a timeline. Generate sample findings in GuardDuty (titles start with [SAMPLE]) to see the structure and severity of an alert. For operations, I would consider a trail that applies to multiple Regions, block public access to the log bucket, and limit who can delete logs. A logging system that an attacker can delete is no longer trustworthy.
My takeaway: CloudTrail answers the question “what happened”, while GuardDuty helps answer “is anything suspicious”. How useful the alerts are has to be verified with a lab in my own account.
References:
Working with CloudTrail event history: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/view-cloudtrail-events.html How CloudTrail works (trail and event history): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/how-cloudtrail-works.html What is Amazon GuardDuty?: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/what-is-guardduty.html Understanding Amazon GuardDuty findings: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_findings.html Generating sample findings in GuardDuty: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/sample_findings.html Pricing in GuardDuty (30-day free trial): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty-pricing.html #AWS #AWSStudyGroup #FCAJ #FirstCloudAIJourney #CloudTrail #GuardDuty #CloudSecurity

title: Security and Well-Architected
content: Security controls in the design Area Control Identity Cognito user pool with an admin group and no self-registration; the admin user is created by a script that asks for the password Authorization JWT authorizer on /admin/* (signature, issuer, audience, expiry); Lambda also checks token_use=access and the admin group, so an ID token is rejected Session HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict and Secure cookie handled by the Next.js BFF; no token in localStorage Least privilege Lambda execution role limited by ARN to the DynamoDB table, the image prefixes in the private S3 bucket and the SES identity Data at rest DynamoDB encryption and point-in-time recovery; private S3 bucket with Block Public Access and SSE-S3 Data in transit HTTPS through Amplify Hosting and API Gateway Input and abuse Schema validation, consent check, honeypot field, IP and email limits with TTL counters, API Gateway throttling, CORS for the exact frontend origin Log privacy The access log keeps no cookies, authorization headers or request bodies Well-Architected view Pillar What the project does Remaining gap Operational excellence CloudFormation templates, access log, dashboard, four alarms and a runbook Alarm actions are not connected to SNS yet Security The controls above No WAF, no admin MFA screen, SES still in the sandbox Reliability On-demand DynamoDB with point-in-time recovery, idempotent reservations, transaction for seat capacity No restore drill, no email queue, one Region Performance efficiency arm64 Lambda with 256 MB, CDN on Amplify Hosting, on-demand capacity No load test yet (target: p95 under 2 s) Cost optimization Pay-per-use services, 14-day log retention, two cost estimates Estimate not yet compared with a real bill Sustainability No idle servers; arm64 functions Not measured

title: Testing, validation and operations
content:
Test results Local: 30 automated tests, TypeScript check and builds pass; the smoke suite on a local build passes 41 HTTP checks (reservation, resubmission, admin authorization, image upload). The DynamoDB transaction is tested with a mock. Backend on AWS: 14 checks pass, covering Cognito access token, rejection of an ID token, saving and reading reservations, status change, idempotency, real S3 PUT/GET and contact messages. Release checks: the public and admin APIs both return 100 dishes, the 7 pages return HTTP 200, and images match byte for byte. These are HTTP checks, not browser automation. Negative requests that anyone can repeat (expected results in brackets):
curl -i "$API_URL/admin/reservations" # 401 curl -i -X POST "$API_URL/reservations" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{}' # 400 curl -i -X POST "$API_URL/reservations" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{bad-json' # 400 Not done yet: a real concurrency test on DynamoDB, a load test (target p95 under 2 s at 5 requests/s for 5 minutes) and a point-in-time-recovery drill. They are planned, not claimed as passed.
Logs API Gateway access log with requestId, requestTime, routeKey, status, responseLength and integrationLatency; no cookies, authorization headers or request bodies. Retention is 14 days. Lambda log group /aws/lambda/aurel-backend-api, plus Amplify build and SSR logs. aws logs tail /aws/lambda/aurel-backend-api --since 10m Metrics and alarms A separate aurel-observability stack creates a dashboard and four CloudWatch alarms:
Alarm Metric Condition LambdaErrors Lambda Errors, Sum at least 1 in 5 minutes LambdaThrottles Lambda Throttles, Sum at least 1 in 5 minutes Api5xx API Gateway 5xx, Sum at least 1 in 5 minutes ApiLatency API Gateway Latency, Average 2000 ms or more in 2 consecutive 5-minute windows Alerts Missing data is treated as not breaching. Alarm actions are still empty and there is no SNS subscription, so the alarms change state in CloudWatch but do not send email yet. A SetAlarmState test moved Api5xx to ALARM and back to OK; this is a simulation, not a real incident.
When an alarm fires Alarm First thing to check LambdaErrors Open the Lambda log group, find the failing call by its request ID, and check whether a deployment just happened LambdaThrottles Check concurrent executions and the account quota, and look for a burst of requests in the access log Api5xx Filter the access log for 5xx rows (routeKey, status), then follow the requestId into the Lambda log ApiLatency Compare integrationLatency with the total latency in the access log, then check Lambda duration and DynamoDB calls

title: Cost estimate and optimization
content:
Assumptions Per month: 10,000 visits, 100,000 API requests and 100,000 SSR requests, 20 GB of delivered content, Lambda 256 MB at 200 ms, 1,000 emails and 5 admin users; Singapore Region, USD, before tax and before free tier.
Estimates Item Monthly cost (USD) AWS Pricing Calculator workload estimate (20 usage lines, 8 services) about 6.00 Independent budget model, including allowances for transfer, dashboard and CodeCommit 12.17 Independent budget with a 25% reserve 15.21 The independent model adds allowances (dashboard, data transfer, CodeCommit, report build) and uses conservative rates, so it is higher than the Calculator figure, which covers only the 20 entered lines. Neither is a bill. Not included: WAF, NAT, SQS, a custom domain, paid support and DynamoDB restore or export.
Optimization measures Use pay-per-use services (Lambda, API Gateway, on-demand DynamoDB) so an idle site costs little. Run Lambda on arm64 with a small memory size and keep log retention at 14 days. Tag resources and set a monthly budget with an email alert before running labs. Clean up unused stacks and the retained resources after each lab (see the clean-up page).

title: Clean-up
content:
Run this only in your own lab account and only after you decide to stop the service. Deleting a stack does not remove everything: the DynamoDB table, the media and artifacts buckets and the CodeCommit repository use the Retain policy.
List the physical resources of each stack (aurel-frontend, aurel-backend, aurel-artifacts, aurel-observability) and note who owns them. Back up data you need and check that the copy can be read. Stop new builds and remove the separate report branch stack if you created one; do not delete a shared Amplify app. Delete the stacks in this order, waiting for DELETE_COMPLETE each time: frontend, backend, observability, then artifacts. aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name aurel-frontend aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name aurel-frontend Handle the Retain resources by hand: for versioned buckets remove all versions, delete markers and multipart uploads before deleting the bucket (a plain recursive remove is not enough), then delete the table and the repository from your inventory. Check Amplify logs, any SNS subscription or Budget you added, and other Regions. Review Billing after the data updates. Do not use wildcards to delete Retain resources and do not touch resources of other projects.

title: Demo, lessons and next steps
content:
Live product Website (Amplify): https://main.d2rkhtb7c0k5r7.amplifyapp.com/ Admin page: https://main.d2rkhtb7c0k5r7.amplifyapp.com/admin Source code: https://github.com/ndthuy21/aurel-restaurant The admin password is not published in this report; the presenter signs in on their own device. Dish names, prices, brand and address are sample data, so do not enter real customer information when trying the demo.
Demo video Watch on YouTube · Team FantasticFive video “Dự án AWS Nhóm FantasticFive”, posted by Huỳnh Trí Nhân on 24/11/2026 (about 4 minutes 21 seconds according to the group’s report). It shows the customer pages, the contact and reservation forms, and the admin screen for managing the menu.
Suggested demo script Introduce the problem and open the architecture diagram. Menu: search, filter and page through the 100 dishes loaded from the API. Reservation form: send a valid request, then a wrong body to show the backend validation. Admin: sign in, open the pending request and change its status. Create a test dish with an image upload and check it on the menu page. Show CloudWatch: request count, 4xx and 5xx, logs and alarms. Questions: SES sandbox, admin MFA, quotas and the proposed email queue. More evidence Photo evidence: the AUREL home page running on Amplify Hosting.
Common problems and fixes Symptom Likely cause What to do Browser shows a CORS error after deployment FrontendOrigin is still https://pending.invalid Redeploy the backend with the real frontend origin Menu is empty or the app cannot reach the API API_BASE_URL or NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL is missing or ends with a slash; NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are fixed at build time Correct the variables and start a new Amplify job /admin/* returns 401 after signing in An ID token was sent, or the access token (valid for 1 hour) expired Sign in again; the BFF must forward the access token A reservation is saved but no email arrives SES is in the sandbox and the recipient is not verified Verify the address or use the mailbox simulator The Amplify job fails Wrong Node version or missing variables Read the build log, use Node 22 and the variable table Resources remain after deleting stacks Retain policy on the table, buckets and repository Follow the clean-up page Font error reported on a Windows machine Fonts and symbols that depend on the device may lack glyphs Embed Noto for Vietnamese, check NFC/NFD, replace symbols with SVG. Not yet re-tested on Windows Documentation commits still trigger a build The pipeline follows the branch and may not honor skip markers Stop jobs that change only documentation; keep the report repository separate from the app Lessons learned Write down every output of a stack right after creating it; later steps depend on them. Keep the deployment package bucket separate from the media bucket. Test the failure paths (401, 400) as well as the happy path. State the limits honestly (SES sandbox, no WAF, no load test) instead of hiding them. Next steps Email outbox with SQS and a dead-letter queue, then SES production access. MFA for the admin, and AWS WAF in front of the API. A load test and a point-in-time recovery drill. SNS notifications for the four alarms.
